speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) is hardly correct when he says that this railroad is being built under the unemployment relief scheme. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on Friday last I was asked a question by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw) as to the proposed method to be used in connection with the collection of the sales tax, and I now desire to make the following statement. A large number of communications have been received from merchants and others respecting the new method of collection. The officials of the department were and still are of the opinion that the method proposed in the resolution will be more effective than that now in use. However, the government is most anxious that the increased sales tax, as to the amount of which not a single complaint has been received, should foe collected with as little inconvenience as possible to the business community. subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSTPONEMENT UNTIL 1932
speechtext:
I had intended, before the orders of the day were called, to make the following statement: In accordance with the resolution of the Imperial conference held at London in 1930, that the economic section of the conference be adjourned to meet at Ottawa on a date within the next twelve months to be

Trans-Canada Highway
mutually agreed upon, in order to resume examination of the various means by which interimperial trade may best be maintained and extended, the Canadian government some time ago proposed that the conference should meet at Ottawa in August of this year. This date was found generally acceptable.. The government of the Commonwealth of Australia have now informed us that in view of the uncertain position in Australia, and considering at the same time the importance of the conference and the desirability of full representation, they would therefore request postponement until next year. The government of New Zealand had previously indicated that in view of the fact that its parliament would be in session in August and of the possibility of general elections towards the end of the year, it was unlikely that New Zealand could be represented by a minister of the crown at a conference to be held in August or, in fact, before 1932. We have therefore brought this situation to the attention of His Majesty's governments in the United Kingdom, the Union of South Africa, the Irish Free State and Newfoundland, as well as the government of India, which had all previously indicated their readiness to attend in August. In reply they have agreed to accept the proposal that the conference should foe postponed until 1932. The conference will therefore be postponed accordingly. At the same time the government avails itself of this opportunity to reaffirm its unquestionable belief in the soundness of the proposals made and the position taken at the conference in London last fall.

BRADETTE (North Timiskaming): Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I want again to direct the attention of the house to a question of national importance, as I believe the Prime Minister will agree when I put the matter before him. Only last week I brought up a discussion of this question in the house, and not a single member can accuse me of having been a 
partisan. To-day there is a situation in northern Ontario which must be faced. Had the Prime Minister understood the question that I put before the house a few momenta ago, I believe he would have answered it. I want to place it again before the house. I refer to a statement made by the Hon. William Finlayson, Minister of Lands and Forests in the Ontario provincial government, at a meeting at Kapuskasing on Tuesday of last week, as reported in the Northern Tribune of Kapuskasing, of June 5, 1931. He made a statement to the effect that an arrangement had been arrived at between the Ontario provincial government and the federal government that three survey parties would go over the ground this season to study the routing of the trans-Canada highway in northern Ontario. Not only the citizens of northern Ontario but those of the whole of Canada are directly interested in the important matter which I have brought to the attention of the house. Again I ask the Prime Minister if really there has been anything done in cooperation with the Ontario government with a view to the construction of the transdUanada highway in northern Ontario. I believe my question is a fair one. I do not wish to delay the business o'f the house; I believe there is no hon. member on either side who will accuse me, either this session or in previous sessions, when I was sitting on the government benches, of taking up too much time. I repeat, however, that because of the unemployment situation in northern Ontario and the necessity of beginning the work this year, my right hon. friend should answer a question which to my mind is absolutely logical and fair.

I am sure the Prime Minister is
not deliberately withholding information from thie House of Commons. If the statement was made by the Minister of Lands and Forests for Ontario to the effect that three survey parties have been sent out, surely hon. members should have such information before them. The people of northern Ontario, irrespective of their political affiliations, are very much interested in the construction of the highway. During the last regular session of parliament the representation was made, when hon. members were discussing the resolution made by Mr. Kellner, that if the government would contribute something toward the construction of the highway thousands of men would receive work immediately and the unemployment situation would be appreciably .relieved. That statement was made by some

Trans-Canada Highway
hon. members of the presenlt government who last year were in opposition. One evening during the last week the present Minister of Railways and Oana-ls (Mr. Manion) stood in his place and said that the matter was still under consideration and that he had nothing definite to say in connection with it. Of course in his own way he endeavoured to ridicule my position. I wish to say to him and to his friends who may advise him that for the past twenty years my stand concerning the highway through northern Ontario has been well known and cannot be ridiculed by him or any other hon. member of the house. The position taken last year by members of the present government was that if the government would contribute money towards the building of a highway, hundreds, perhaps thousands, of men would be put to work during the winter. Yet only a few days ago the Minister of Railways and Canals admitted that there is unemployment in northern Ontario due in a large measure to conditions in the pulip and paper industry. I am not going to deliver a speech upon this question but when the Minister of Railways and Canals says the matter is under consideration and a minister of a provincial government, the Minister of Lands and Forests in Ontario, makes the statement that the dominion government has agreed, in cooperation with the provincial government to send out survey parties, I think an explanation should be made. If this government has agreed with the provincial government to survey three different routes, hon. members in the house want to know it and they have a right to know it. If such an arrangement has not been made we would like to know if Mr. Finlayson is up in northern Ontario telling them onie more of the poppycock stories he has been telling for many years. I am inclined to think that probably he is just telling another story. Every time he goes to northern Ontario he tells a different dtory with respect to intended procedure concerning the highway through that country During all this time there are hundreds and thousands of men unemployed through the northern section of Ontario.

speechtext: There is quite a difference.

Hon. members want to know what is being done. I would be inclined to move an amendment to the motion to go into supply in order to have an expression from the house in respect to this highway question. During the election campaign the present government stated that under their administration a national highway would be built. Mr. Ferguson made the statement that the building of such a highway was a national question and not one of provincial obligation. Mr. Finlayson said the question was national in obligation. However, at the present time we learn that although he is acting as if it is a provincial question and they are working in cooperation with the dominion government. With my hon friends from northern Ontario on this side of the house I want to know how long we are going to be kept in the position of playing politics in connection with the question of highways and byways through northern Ontario. An opportunity is now afforded the government to tell us whether or not they have an agreement with the provincial government to make surveys. If they have I would be quite agreeable; if a highway is going to be built through the efforts of the administration at Ottawa I would be satisfied. If it is to be built by contribution to the provincial government I would be satisfied. No matter what is going to be done, I would like to see some action taken. I do not however want to see one party saying the matter is under consideration and in the very next breath the minister of a provincial government saying there is an agreement to send out survey parties throughout northern Ontario.

I rise, Mr. Speaker, to put on record a report in the Ottawa Journal concerning a statement made by the Hon. William Finlayson:
The Ontario government through the Department of Lands and Forests will undertake^ a complete survey of the various alternative routes, with a view to determining the cost of construction and value from settlement and tourist standpoints.
Three Surveys
This will entail at least three reconnaissance surveys, one to examine the proposed location west of Sault Ste. Marie, along the shore of lake Superior, another to examine the proposed northern route, from Nipigon east to Hearst and a third to give its attention to the proposed "compromise" route. Reconnaissance parties are being organized at the present time and surveys will be proceeded with at the earliest possible date.
This announcement was made here to-night by Hon. William Finlayson, Minister of Lands and Forests in the Ontario government, at the close of his annual tour of the north country.
In the report contained in the Journal the Hon. William Finlayson does not mention the federal government whatsoever.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That makes it worse.
Unemployment-Mr. Neill

I think I was straining politeness when I said what I did. However, for the present, I shall not allude further to the banned question of unemployment. I will leave it to the judgment of the country.
I now wish to call the attention of the house to a growing serious public sentiment in certain sections of the west, which if not paid attention to and guarded against, so to speak, will possibly, and I believe quite credibly, threaten civil riot and possibly social revolution in the near future. I can perhaps best illustrate that sentiment by reading a letter that I received the other day from a man whom I know to be of high character and high attainments. He has two professions at least at his finger ends. He writes me as follows from Vancouver:
I noted your speech regarding the conditions in Nanaimo, and from the first hand information of my own, I can fully confirm all you said.
Your speech has caused me to wonder if you are as well informed as to what is being said and felt in Vancouver, and perhaps the following may interest you somewhat. I may say I have been living here since November, and my work has brought me in daily contact with all classes and conditions of people; further, during this time I have been consistently sounding people's opinions and feelings about the present and the future.
May I interject here that this man is a professional man, and is therefore naturally associating with people of that class, and the remarks he cites are not those of the logger or longshoreman, but those of people in a ' position to judge, and not at all likely to run away with bolshevik ideas. He continues:
Several features of these expressions of opinion are most arresting. The most startling and common one expressed is a deep-seated and genuine fear that we will never come out of the present impasse without disturbances which will probably be the beginning of a real civil war between the "haves" and the "have liots." I want to emphasize that this is not from the "down and outs" but comes just as frequently from business people.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

These sentiments are common among educated, business and professional men. There are many more such statements I could quote, if my memory allowed. When we find business and commercial men, men who have a stake in the country, men who are not animated by political motives, using expressions such as that, there is some reason to reflect on what lies behind their statements. I think hon. members will admit that bishops, generally speaking, are not inclined to be bolshevik or communistic. We find one bishop however telling his clergy to take care, and go down and visit the jungles. Do you know what a jungle is, Mr. Deputy Speaker? I do not think you do; as a matter of fact I do not think many hon. members do.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

The hon. member is
going too far.

A few days ago I had a resolution forwarded to me from the synod meeting of a church. May I add that in the dictionary sense of the word, the church is a conservative body. They forwarded a resolution saying that we must do something to meet social conditions or we cannot adhere to the doctrines of Christ, or words to that effect. I would refer hon. members to the statement of a well known man in the city of Vancouver who said, "Why not get down to a coalition government such as we had during the war. Why not get down to business, without scrapping about politics while people are starving." In reply to those queries that gentleman received the fallowing answer:
Unless the government do something there will be chaos this winter, or something worse.
That man, an alderman of the city of Vancouver, was not playing up to bolsheviks. I feel I must warn the government indirectly, if not directly, that some action ought to be taken to deal with conditions which are continually getting worse.
Why not get down to business?

At this time I would ask .the Prime Minister for some information. He is asking for a certain amount of money in connection with the Maritime Freight Rates Act. A few days ago a discussion arose in committee, and hon. members did not know where we stood in the matter. On the order paper there is a resolution providing for $68,-

Interim Supply Bill

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I would ask my -hon.
friend to look at items 379, 380, 381, 382 of the estimates; No. 379 referring to loan to Canadian Government Merchant Marine; No. 380 to loan to Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships and Nos. 381 and 382 to the Maritime Freight Rates Act-the first to differentiate between tariff tolls and normal tolls, and the other to pay for an increased deficit over what was contemplated for 1931.
I suppose my hon. friend is reading from the bill?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, I am referring to the main estimates as tabled-379, 380, 381 and 382.

We have not got

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, my hon. friend has them. This is entirely separate.
This is an entirely new procedure. That is why we want to know about it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend is right
as to that. The bill authorizing the company to create an issue of securities for 868,000,000 odd, or of such other sum as may be recommended by the committee, also provides, as he will recall, for the guaranteeing of those securities. I took the view when I was in opposition, and I take it now, that moneys thus obtained cannot be said to be supply voted to His Majesty, but are moneys which the company are obtaining on the guarantee of the country, the securities being floated by the company on the security of the governor in council. That is the distinction. The one is by supply bill, the other by a bill the same as by any other company, with the guarantee of the country attached.

The Minister of
Railways (Mr. Manion) misled the committee to a certain extent, or perhaps he misunderstood the circumstances. He informed the committee first of all that the resolution on the order paper in the name of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Bennett) to provide for
868,000,000 odd was to be discussed and a bill based on that resolution would then be introduced by the Minister of Finance himself. Then he informed us that Bill No. 79 was in lieu of the estimates of the capital expenditure for last year of the Canadian National Railways. If this is correct, the title would indicate that the Minister of Railways should have preceded the bill by a resolution.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It was introduced by a
resolution.
No.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The bill was.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I moved the resolution.
Would the resolution introduced by the Minister of Finance apply to the bill introduced by the Minister of Railways and Canals?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Perhaps my hon. friend
will follow me in this explanation. 1. The railway company, as such, introduces a bill which requires no resolution. If is a private corporation introducing its bill. 2. The Minister of Finance has introduced a resolution, which resolution has received the approval of His Excellency and is now upon the order paper. That resolution provides for a guarantee being given to the securities of the Canadian National Railways, and if my hon. friend will be good enough to look at the estimates he will see that the four items to which reference is made do not in any sense deal with the matters dealt with by the bill. The matters referred to in the four items are: Loan to the Canadian National Steamships; loan to the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships; amount required to meet difference between tariff tolls and normal tolls under the Maritime Freight Rates Act; amount required to provide for the payment from time to time, to the Canadian National Railway Company of the deficit in receipts and revenues, occurring during the year 1931, of the eastern lines, as provided by the Maritime Freight Rates Act.
I am sorry to worry the Prime Minister but I am seeking information.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Quite so.

I was surprised myself when the Minister of Railways stated in committee that Bill No. 79 took the place of the estimates of the Canadian National Railways of capital expenditure for last year. He said that this was not a money bill. If you look at the title of the bill you will see that it is:
An act respecting the Canadian National Railways and to authorize the provision of moneys to meet expenditures made and indebtedness incurred during the calendar year 1931.
Surely, sir, that is a money bill.

Interim, Supply Bill

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No. My hon. friend is
quite right in thinking that we have entirely departed from the practice heretofore prevailing. If he wild look at the explanatory note he will find it is in these words:
The object of this bill is to authorize the Canadian National Railways Company to issue securities to the extent of $68,500,000 for the purpose, during the year 1931, of financing where the amounts available from net operating income or investments may be insufficient.
That is not a money bill any more than a bill for the issue of securities by the Canadian Pacific Railway or any other railway company is a money bill. It puts the Canadian National Railway Company in exactly the same position as any other railway company. The Canadian National Railway Company seeks the authority of this parliament to issue securities to the extent of $68,500,000, just as the Minister of Railways said, or such lesser sums as the special committee may conclude, after its investigations are completed, would be adequate, having regard to the services to be rendered in 1931. It is not a money bill, I repeat.
Does the Prime Minister object to my continuing the discussion?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

Last session the financial requirements of the Canadian National Railways were introduced in the form of estimates. I want to call the attention of the Prime Minister to this. Last year in the estimates we simply authorized the Canadian National Railway Company to float loans in four different ways: 1, from the treasury; 2, publicly without guarantee; 3, publicly with guarantee; 4, temporarily. By this bill you are creating first of all a new term, "authorized expenditures." I suppose it should have been "statutory expenditures." Then the other section would not have been embodied in the bill. But outside of that you are creating a new departure by dividing under three different headings the total amount of $68,500,000, which is also the amount mentioned in the resolution moved by the Minister of Finance. The methods of allowing the company to raise loans are absolutely different from what they were last year. I agree entirely with what the Prime Minister is doing, and I should like to go a little further, touching section 3. Under that section the governor in council controls absolutely the issue of any securities of any kind that may be raised by the Canadian National Railways; everything is done subject to the approval of the governor in council. I remember a discussion we had in the committee three years ago, and we came to the conclusion then that the ideal system would be for the government to raise money and be the only creditor of the Canadian National Railways. Should this course be followed, I, for one, would support it. But it appears to me that there should be a change in the heading, because as now headed it is a money bill; and if it is a money bill it should be introduced by a resolution. Of course, I trust entirely not only the judgment but the statement of the Prime Minister, but I should like to have this point cleared up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend has observed the difference between the method adopted heretofore, and the method which we propose to adopt in connection with the raising of moneys for the Canadian National Railways undertaking. He says he agrees with the views we have put forward in the legislation in question, and I think that the judgment of the house will concur with him in that regard. The supply bills of the country always begin, "Most Gracious Sovereign: Whereas it appears", and then in the schedule that was attached last year there is a statement of the sum required for railways. We now propose that the Canadian National Railways shall be exactly as any other railway enterprise. It seeks the authority of this parliament to issue its securities to the amount stated in the bill. My hon, friend suggests that this might be designated as a money bill because of t'he title: "An Act respecting the Canadian National Railways and to authorize the provision of moneys to meet expenditures made and indebtedness incurred during the calendar year 1931." If the title is regarded as not truly designating the purport of the bill, it can, of course, be amended. But I think that upon investigation my hon. friend will conclude that the title properly designates the provisions of the bill, for the bill provides merely for the authorization of the right on the part of the company to create securities.

I am not speaking for myself alone; this discussion took place in committee. What surprised us to a certain extent was the fact that in this bill there appear the words "authorized expenditure", and authorized expenditure is defined throughout the bill. It will be found that for the first time this year the estimates of the Canadian National Railways, instead of being voted en bloc, are divided into three parts- $31,000,000, $9,000,000 and $27,000,000. It is apparently intended that there shall be no transfer of one vote to another without
Interim Supply Bill

authority. But it will be observed that authorization is given in paragraph (c) of section 2, to switch any desired portion of the sum mentioned in that paragraph to the purposes indicated in paragraph (a). I regret this very much, and I am sorry also that the subdivision of the vote has not been carried further. In the old estimates there were a number of headings under which this vote could have been divided, and I think it would be not only to the interest of parliament but to the interest of the committee as well if the subdivision were carried further. Information will have to be furnished the committee in toto with regard to every one of these items, and the more it is subdivided the less danger there is of switching. As regards the methods adopted I have only one regret- they do not go far enough.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The government will be indeed very much satisfied if the committee in the exercise of its judgment concludes to attach to the bill a schedule, dividing it into as many items as it deems advisable. There is no desire in any sense to lessen the activities of the committee in making recommendations, and so far as dividing the estimates is concerned, I assure my hon. friend that he may divide them into thirty parts if he wishes. When the bill is given its second reading it will be referred to a special committee with power to deal with it in any way they consider in the public interest. In other words, they may increase the number of items to as many as they think desirable.

Will the Prime Minister answer another question? I am seeking general information with a view to the discussion in committee. I understand that this will take the place of the ordinary estimates of the Candian National Railways. Will the bill introduced by the Minister of Finance, based on the resolution with respect to the $68,000,000, be submitted to the committee for discussion?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It was not intended that that bill should be sent to the committee for discussion. After the committee has made its report that bill will be proceeded with, and it will represent only the amount which the .icnimittee reports as desirable. There will be no point in considering that bill, the members of the committee having done their duty when they have concluded what sum shall be appropriated. The Minister of Finance will then bring in his bill in accordance with that of the Minister of Railways.
tSir Eugene Fiset.]
The provision by this parliament of $68,000,000 is dealt with in Bill No. 79. Apart from that, provision is made in the ordinary estimates for the deficit on the eastern line, for the Marine^-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They are statutory obligations.

The relation between the resolution of the Minister of Finance with respect to the $68,000,000 and these other details is rather a complicated one. It is the first time such a departure is being made. We have a few new members on the committee, and if for this year the two bills were submitted to the committee at the same time for study we should be better able to understand the relationship between the bill not based upon a resolution and that introduced by the Minister of Finance preceded by resolution.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I assure the hon. gentleman that the bills will provide the same amount. One will provide for the guarantee and the other for the authorization of the issue of securities. Whatever is thought desirable to enable the committee to be thoroughly seized with the situation the government will be glad to have done.
Is it the intention not to present to parliament the estimates of the Canadian National Railways?

speechtext:
The estimates of the
Canadian National Railways are contained in the bill.

In this bill
which is down now?

speechtext: In the bill of the Minister of Railways. The Canadian National Railways divide 'their financial operations under two heads: (a) statutory obligations of the country as disclosed in the estimates, 379, 380, 381, 382,-'that is, steamship lines, the West India line, the Freight Rates Act-

speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.

Ways and Means-Interim Supply

That is my
point.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Then come the estimates of the Canadian National Railways as indicated by Bill No. 79. That is referred to the committee. It refers to the construction program of the road and its maintenance, the acquisition of securities, and matters of that kind. Then comes the bill by the government to enable the guarantee to be given for the sum which the committee reports it is necessary to raise this year for the system. In other words, the resolution that is now before the house in my name is a resolution preceding the bill which fixes the country's liability. The other bill is exactly similar to that of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Algoma Central, and other roads; only in one instance 'it is referred to a special committee instead of to the railway committee. That special committee's report may diminish to some extent the amount of the estimates of the railway. In that event the two will correspond: they will provide exactly the same amount. Whatever amount the railway company succeeds in convincing the railway committee would be a proper estimate for the year will be the amount for which guarantee will be given after authorization by this parliament of the bill which stands in the name of tihe Minister of Finance.

The misunderstanding arose when the Minister of Railways, in introducing his bill, made the statement that it related to railway estimates of the Canadian National Railways. The words of Hansard are:
This bill. Mr. Speaker, is to authorize the Canadian National Railways to issue securities to cover $68,500,000, being the amount of the estimate of the railways' deficiency in their needs above .their earnings for 1931: really the estimates of the Canadian National Railways.
That last clause possibly was an afterthought on the minister's part. The estimates now before the committee will be referred to the railway committee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I was not here when the minister made the statement. The. first part is obviously correct. The second part with respect to the deficit is covered by the estimates submitted to the House of Commons, because under the statutes this country, whether or not we like it, has to provide that money out of consolidated revenue, and that is the reason why it is in our estimates as distinct from being in the bill. I believe there was some doubt among the legal officers as to just what was the meaning of the words in the original statute and last year, as perhaps my right hon. friend will recall, the railway
company issued its securities to take care of its deficits guaranteed by the dominion under authority conferred by parliament at its last session. The distinction I have been endeavouring ito make is the distinction between supply and providing for the requirements of the railway. While I was in opposition I mentioned this matter, although not in great detail. I think there is a clear distinction between supply to His Majesty and the provision of the necessary authority for the railway company to issue its securities. As long as we do it by the indirect method as mentioned by the hon. member for Rimouski, so long I think it should be done by separate and distinct legislation, the one conferring authority and the other authorizing the guarantee. The other items to which my right hon. friend has just referred clearly are items of supply and I think my colleague for a moment dealt with the deficit as being included in the authorizing Bill No. 79. That is not quite correct as that is dealt with by the estimates themselves.
Is it the intention to continue this procedure in the future?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I propose to follow that principle; it may be possible we can improve upon it but I have no intention to revert to supply except for those items that create statutory obligations of the country to the railway.
Will the hon. minister allow the resolution to stand until a final report is received from the committee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This interim supply has nothing to do with that.
I was referring to the other resolution.

With the consent of the house, I will put the resolution through, have it read the first and second time, and then allow it to rest until such time as the committee has made its report. Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State) moved that the house go into committee on Bill No. 4, to amend the Copyright Act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

May I be permitted to say
on the motion to adopt section 1, that the bill as introduced into the house has been considered by a select committee appointed for that purpose and representative of all parties in the house, and it has been reported with certain amendments. I may say generally that the committee was unanimous in its opinion with regard to this bill. One member of the committee, the hon. member for Ottawa, reserved the right to discuss one or two sections with which he was not fully in accord.

The general scope of the bill seeks, bj' amending the definitions, to enlarge the application of section 4 of the Copyright Act which provides that:
Copyright shall subsist in Canada for the term hereinafter mentioned, in every original, literary, dramatic, musical and artistic work.
In the definition we have defined more clearly the words:
Original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic work.
in order to include within the scope of the bill the works which are protected or proposed to be protected by the Rome copyright convention, to which it is suggested, under the provisions of this bill, that Canada shall adhere. The government has received notice from the government of the United Kingdom that, on behalf of that government, the Rome copyright convention will be ratified before the first of July next, which is the last day of the term within which ratification is possible. I am bringing this bill to the attention of the committee this afternoon in the hope that if it meets the approval of the house, it may be placed before the Senate at an early date, because the bill in the form in which it is finally enacted must receive the approval of His Majesty early in June, as at least ten days will be required in order to give notice of ratification on behalf of Canada. Therefore the matter is one of some urgency if Canada is to adhere to the Rome copyright convention which was signed by representatives of the government of Canada during the regime of the present leader of the opposition.
The bill itself, if I may be allowed to explain, provides in every clause except two, namely, 6 and 10 of the amended bill, amendments which have been asked for on behalf of authors. In other respects I think it enlarges the scope of our present act and gives greater security to the authors than has ever before been given by legislation in Canada. Sections 6 and 10 are regulative. They are the sections which have caused discussion.

Perhaps I may be permitted, on section 1, to say a few words of a general character. I endorse fully what the Secretary of State has just said. The main purpose of the bill is to bring the act into conformity with the convention at Rome, but in doing so, especially in enacting section 9 which does away with compulsory registration, we met with conditions in this country which perhaps also require a little attention. If hon. gentlemen read schedule A which reproduces the Rome copyright convention, they will see that while the convention has laid down certain general principles, a number of

Copyright Act
Which issue from former conventions, it has also left to every country a certain degree of freedom in legislating for domestic purposes. I believe the bill comes very strictly within that interpretation. It corrects certain omissions or defects of the act as it stands now and at the same time it has made an effort to meet the conditions which will be created by the new enactment.
If I were to write a treatise on copyright, if I may put it in that Way, or give my theories as to copyright, I might make some reservations as to certain sections, for instance, sections 6 and 10, which take away from the owner of 'the copyright partial enjoyment of his rights. But I know all the conditions; I have been in charge of similar legislation for a number of years, and I think the bill is most excellent in that iit meets all conditions and comes strictly within the convention as to its principles whilst iit makes an effort to adjust conditions created in Canada by adherence to the Rome convention.
Perhaps I may be permitted to say that although I have sat on a number of committees on copyright, I have never before been on one where there has 'been such an excellent spirit of cooperation on the part of members of the three parties in the house, and it is a great pleasure to me to pay tribute to the Secretary of State for the open-minded and impartial way in which he conducted all the meetings. So far as I am concerned I do not hesitate ito commend the bill to my hon. friends on this side of the house.

It is not my intention
to speak at any length on all of the clauses of this bill. I desire, however, to express some difference of opinion with regard to certain remarks that have been made by the minister who introduced the bill, especially wherein he says that most of its provisions represent demands made by the authors themselves. I represent no particular interest. When I sat in the select committee I did not represent the interests of authors, no antagonistic interests, nor did anybody on the committee represent any special interests. I think I can show, in the course of my remarks with respect to particular sections of the bill, as they are called, that though the bill may go some little distance, it can by no means be regarded as highly desirable legislation from the point of view of the protection of authors' organizations at the same time not interfering in any way with the legitimate interests of others.

May I say that in these
amendments we have complied with many of the requests of the authors and of various
international societies and others who asked for amendments?

I cannot accept that reservation. In so far as the other statement of the hon. Secretary of State goes, that this bill grants more security, I deplore that it does not, and I shall show that in my comments on the various sections as they are called; for I presume it is the intention of the committee that the sections shall be called and studied one by one.
It might not be amiss at this moment to say a word or two on just what copyright is. I do not pretend, and it is not my intention at this time, nor is this the place, to make any long discourse on that point. Indeed I would not introduce that subject were it not for the fact that since the bill was introduced and since the select committee considered it, hon. members have spoken to me about certain features of it, some of them expressed considerable surprise-I say this without any thought of hurting the susceptibilities of anyone-that there was a fundamental difference between the right of property in a work, as defined under the statute, and in a house, a horse, a farm, a chair, or any other chattel or real property.
I shall not go back to the time of the origin of copyright, but there is an idea prevailing to-day, which is a very erroneous one, and which leads to much difficulty in interpretation and in the settlement of rights, that copyright is purely and simply a statutory right. That is not by any means so. Copyright is as old as any other right of property, but unfortunately this right has been limited and constantly pruned down by statutes. Let me say this once more, that if parliament has the right to limit the enjoyment of copyright, as undoubtedly parliament has, and if parliament wants to reduce that right, to take away 95 per cent of the rights of the authors and grant them only the remaining 5 per cent of their rights by statute, then let parliament at the same time grant to the owners of that 5 per cent residue, 100 per cent enjoyment of the rights of ownership in that 5 per cent. I have no hesitation in affirming, and I shall prove it as I go along, that the en-j oyment of those rights has been limited; and all through the present law, and throughout this bill, there is nothing in the way of efficient safeguards, no means of redress for Canadian authors in our own domestic legislation, and far less in connection with the requirements of the Berne convention revised at Rome, to which we are about to signify our ratification. It may be of interest to the committee, to
Copyright Act

know that, even in the early days of the colony in Canada, copyright amongst the Indians was recognized. I had some years ago the opportunity of going into this matter, and I shall simply give to the committee one or two illustrations for the benefit of those who may think that copyright is a right similar to the right in property.
If we go 'back to 1636, we find by volume 7, page 16, of Jesuits Relations, 1636, that each Indian had his own song, which no other Indian dared to sing otherwise than to the great offence of its composer, and that is why to sing another's song constituted a challenge. Each had his own song, and of his own making, and no one could sing it without insulting the owner and receiving in return a blow from the tomahawk. That was what we would call to-day an infringement of copyright, and that was their method of redress. I would say that, in the bill under review and in the law as it stands, our legislation is sorely deficient in the way of remedies. The Indian's song could not be sung even after his death, except on great festival occasions, and then only by members of the family of the deceased. That showed that protection existed in those days even after the author was dead. La Potherie and Nicolas Perrot relate similar examples of copyright protection among the Indians of the early days of Canada.
I will give one more illustration, going back to the Ammassalik Eskimo, I quote from page 550, volume 40, of East Greenland Nations in Meddelelserom Gronland:
He (the Eskimo) has a monopoly of the song.
Perhaps my hon. friend the minister will frown on the use of this word "monopoly", which he does not like; but monopoly goes back to the time of the Eskimos, monopoly meaning the full right in his song. He had a monopoly of the song, with its text and melody as long as he lived. It was only after his death that it was considered suitable for others to use the particular song and melody which were his. I could go on and give further picturesque illustrations. But I will stop at that.
I should like now to address my remarks to the first clause of the bill. I intend to treat this matter having in mind the words of a great French philosopher, Auguste Comte, who said that "liberty of conscience does not exist in astronomy", meaning that truth is eternal, and that you cannot contemplate any compromise in the light of it. In this matter, I do not intend to stand by any compromise. Copyright is an intricate

and complicated, but most interesting matter; and if at some stages in this discussion I may seem to ramble, I do ask the indulgence of the committee.
So far as copyright is concerned, Canada, in 1921, adhered to the Berne convention of 1886 as revised at Berlin in 1908. We signed the declaration to adhere to the new convention as revised in Rome in 1928, which we are now about to ratify.
I must take issue, very respectfully, with what the hon. Secretary of State said a moment ago as to the intention of this bill. May I assure the committee at once that it is not my intention to oppose its passage. I am quite anxious to see it go through, with the reservations that I shall make, because I feel that some remarks may come later on which will justify the stand that I take now, that this bill does not go far enough to make our present copyright law conform to the stipulations and prescriptions of the Rome convention. I read the following from the explanatory note attached to the bill:
"This bill is not intended to revise generally the Copyright Act, but to amend that act only in so far as is necessary to bring Canadian Copyright legislation into conformity with the provisions of the Rome convention."
I dhould have hoped that the bill would go far enough to do that. However, it does not. As the various clauses are called concerning which I have remarks to make, I will endeavour to make my statements clear.
This is a copyright bill; that is, a bill for the protection of authors. There is the act relating to Patents of Invention passed for the protection of inventors; there is the Trade Marks and Industrial Designs Act for the protection of those who may have industrial designs to protect; there is the Wage Earners Lien Act, and there is the criminal code for the protection 'of citizens against evil-minded people. Then there as the Copyright Act, and I will go so far as to say that it protects nearly everybody but the author himself. If in some respects it does .protect him, it fails to grant rights of recourses which leave the infringement of his right without remedy. I shall endeavour to show, clause by clause, that my statement is correct.
In order to lay the foundation for some of the statements I shall make later on, I should like to refer to some portions of the evidence adduced before the select committee which dealt with Bill No. 4. Probably the quotation of this evidence will prove tiresome, but I think the committee will find some of the extracts most interesting, and they will be in a position to form a proper appreciation of the nature of this most important legislation.

Copyright Act
Would it not be well to cite the evidence as we proceed, clause by clause?

Yes, but there are certain parts of the evidence I should like to cite now. Under clause 1 of the 'bill, I shall make some observations so as not unduly to clutter up the record when the other clauses are reached.
I said that this bill was to protect authors without prejudicially affecting the interests of anyone. I wish at this time to quote an extract from the evidence taken before the committee. At page 33 I find that Mr. George Buck was called and sworn, and I read the folowing from his evidence:
By the Chairman:
Q. Where is your residence, Mr. Buck.-A. In New York. Kensington, Great Neck, Long Island. I am vice-president of the Canadian Performing Right Society, president of the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers.
Later on the evidence is as follows:
"I am not a lawyer, sir. I happen to be an author. I have written for the Ziegfield Follies for some seventeen years."
Then at page 34 I find the following:
"It seems that among some people, and among some nations that those who chose to work with the products of their brains instead of their hands are always begging and heeding to protect that particular gift that they have. If a man makes this chair it is his, no question about it. He does not have to put his name on it, he does not have to register it. But if you choose, sir, to write a song, or a play, or a book or an article, through some particular trick of fate you must go through a million formalities, yet any person loaded with larceny can come along and take it without even asking you any question."
Then at page 35 I read:
"But Mr. Chairman, the desire before this committee that ran rampant through it, that brought me here, sir, was the desire to protect the author,-there would not be a picture house open in America to-night, there would not be a radio set open to-night; there would not be a cabaret or a dance hall open to-night, nor would a state fair open if they did not have bands and music to help put that state fair over, sir."
Then at page 37 I read part of a paragraph which indicates what has to be considered when a bill of this nature is formed:
"That is what brings me here, sir, to make a plea for those men. What other authors are in this room? What other authors are here? Who are the public in this room? The public is not here sir. You gentlemen represent the public. But there is no number of the great public of this nation of this dominion in this room telling you gentlemen to do this. You are only asked to do it by a single group of men who would like to regulate us. That is the basis stripped of all its verbiage, and no one is here to tell them that they shall charge so much an hour: no one is here to tell them that they shall charge so much a seat. And even if those gentlemen are given the right
to regulate their raw material they shall not let the public into the theatre any cheaper. As far as the public is concerned, however, in this particular day of copyright-and if you men know anything about copyright or its ramification, it is the user of the creator, and I appear before you, sir, and you gentlemen, to make the earnest plea for the creator, because through the history of the world, 90 per cent of them are starving to death."
The hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) then asked the question:
How does this bill affect the creator?
And the reply was made:
"Because it shall regulate him and shall not regulate the user."
At this time I shall read from the evidence of Mr. Gitz Rice:
"I am Lieutenant Gitz Rice of the 1st Canadian contingent, a resident of the city of Montreal, a Canadian composer. I took to the profession of song writing before the war, in Canada, and furthered it in France and carried on back here after the war. Since I started my profession of song writing, I have been very fortunate in writing some of the world war's greatest songs. I have yet to collect the first cent from my own country, Canada, for them. I am here as Exhibit A, victim No. 1. I understand, sir. that you are going to put some things in this bill. There has been a lot of squabbling about churches, and a lot of things that I have laughed at many times. The composer always gets the worst of it no matter where you go."
Then Mr. Rice told of the troubles he had had with the gramophone industry as a result of which he secured a judgment for 811,000, which sum was all eaten up in costs. The paragraph ends as follows:
"In fact, if I have to sue all that you wish me to collect in Canada I will be up here for the rest of the days of my life. I do not like this individual suit."
Then, I find the following in the evidence of Mr. Riee:
"I will give you a little example of why I do not like it: An infringement was made on a writing of mine in the city of New York by a big motion picture concern. I went to a legal man, gave him a deposit, and after a few weeks I was told 'don't you think you had better lay off this corporation if you expect to ever do any business with them.' I laid off. I have no enmity against anybody, but I would like to have the chance, as a Canadian, to say how much shall be paid me for my work."
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock, I was about to quote, from page 77, further portions of

the evidence of Mr. Gitz Rice. At the top of the page will be found the following:
"I have never had it up to date, and the only way that I have ever been able to get anything out of it was to associate myself with the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers. The only moneys I have ever derived have been from that society. It is functioning beautifully and we fellows, as composers, have nothing to say against our board of directors for the way in which they have handled our affairs."
Then at page 78:
"It may not include it, sir, because in France in 1915 I created 'Mademoiselle From Armentiores' you know-'Hinky Pinky Parley Voo.' It swept the country. I was at war and doing the best I could with the battery. I could never copyright, you can understand that. And it has swept the country since, and I have yet to earn the first penny from that song. I did not know when I wrote it that it was going to be a hit."
And at the bottom of page 79:
"The Witness: Have you any objection to my retaining and owning my own copyright.

I think that represents the attitude and the state of mind of those for whose benefit this Copyright Act was originally framed, and for whose benefit this bill is supposed to be introduced for the purpose of bringing our law into conformity with the Rome convention. I desire now to proceed to discuss article 4 of the convention itself.
Mr, CAHAN: If we are going to discuss the articles, will it not be advisablfe to deal with them when we come to the schedule?
That is the rule, but as the hon. gentleman was discussing general principles I allowed him to proceed.

I shall be through with this clause in a minute or two. I was trying to lay a general foundation, so that when I came to the other clause, I would not have to clutter up the record with citations of evidence. Now, in order to lay that foundation properly, I want to refer to article 4 of the convention itself, which appears at page 8 of
fMr. Chevrier.]
the bill. There are two kinds of rights mentioned there which are the subject matter of this legislation. This is paragraph (1) of article 4:
Authors who are nationals of any of the countries of the union shall enjoy in countries other than the country of origin of the work, for their works, whether unpublished or first published in a country of the union, the rights which the respective laws do now or may hereafter grant to natives, as well as the rights specially granted by the present convention.
Meaning thereby that there are two kinds of rights in contemplation in this matter: the rights which the natives-the nationals-of Canada now enjoy by virtue of the present Copyright Act; and, further, the rights which the nationals of Canada enjoy in Canada by reason of the Berne convention as it presently is; as well as the rights of any of the contracting parties to that convention which they enjoy in Canada. It is therefore incumbent upon Canada, in the passing of this legislation, to enact such measures as will protect the acquired and vested rights of Canadian nationals, as well as the further rights that may be granted to them under the convention, and the further rights of the unionist authors that come in ipso facto.
In order to save time I will conclude my remarks on this clause by analysing the effect of the bill. Let us see what it does. It amends the present law by adding definitions that have some value, as in section 2. It clarifies certain sections of our law, as in clause 3 and 4, to which I have no objection. It adds a new feature recognized by the Rome convention with reference to "moral right", with which I agree, but which, as I shall show by clause 5, does not go far enough. It tries to regulate certain rights of recourse, but falls far short of giving to the authors, either nationals or unionists, those rights of recourse prescribed by the act, and particularly by the convention to which we have subscribed. It introduces new and vital encroachments on author's rights, as will be found in clauses 6 and 10. It decreases, but does not wipe out, certain formalities imposed upon the enjoyment of rights under clause 10. But it does not remove certain and most objectionable features that are still in the present law.
For those reasons, I conclude my remarks on this clailse by stating that I cannot subscribe to the explanatory note to the effect that this bill amends the Act, namely the Copyright Act, only in so far as it is necessary to bring the Canadian Copyright legislation into conformity with the provisions of the Rome con-

Copyright Act
vention. Some iforty-odd nations have to ratify the convention. They are all unanimous as to the legislation that is to be adopted, and into that concert of nations-I am not saying this in any spirit of levity-I hesitate to see Canada enter with a non-harmonious and non-musical instrument such as the Canadian Copyright Act will become if these amendments are enacted.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Literary, dramatic, musical and artistic work.
Mr. CAHAiN:	With regard to this clause,
the definition, as I explained before, is clarified, and in addition in subsection (2) there is a definition of "legal representatives." Our present act says:
"Legal representatives" includes heirs, executors, administrators, and assigns or other legal representatives."
Doubt has arisen in our courts as to who are constituted "legal representatives." It is a very broad term. Instead of "legal representatives" we have inserted after "administrators" the word "successors" and then we have added "or agents or attorneys who are thereunto duly authorized in writing." I am instructed thait these words clarify the section and make it clear who are legal representatives within the meaning of the statute. That is the only change.

Subsection 3 of
section 2 refers to visual representations of any dramatic action in a work. What protection is accorded anywhere in this bill to dramatic ownership in any dramatic rights, in any dramatic composition? I do not ask this question in a critical spirit. I simply wish to be informed whether there is anything in the bill to ensure such protection.

The act as it now stands
affords the same protection in regard to performances as is given in the English law, and we have added to our definition the words "or by radio communication." In England, the courts have decided that radio communication comes within the meaning of the word performance; but in order to make it clear that the author's rights include not only the right of performance by acoustic representation and so forth, but also by radio communication, we have added those words "or by radio communication" to the present definition of performances as contained in the act. With respect to the protection to which my hon. friend refers, that is ensured by the entire act. I am simply adding the words "or by radio communication" to make it dear that in respect of radio communication the author has exactly the same rights as he has in relation to other performances of his work.

I am sure that the thanks not only of this house but of the whole country must be very, very cordially extended to my hon. friend for the splendid self-sacrificing work he has done in connection with this bill, and I am among the very first to recognize that and to hail him. I hope my hon. friend will appreciate that I do not in any sense fail to realize . what splendid work has been done in this bill which he has brought down. But I desire to know whether it can be shown what protection is accorded the author of any dramatic or musical composition. I mention this because it is a matter of common knowledge, among those who have to deal with such things as a means of livelihood, that the ordinary provision, "you shall restrain by injunctive process, or you shall fine, or do this, that or the other thing if the act is infringed upon" is not applicable and is certainly not operative with respect to legislation such as we have before us. The acts which are in force in the United States are by no means perfect, but they have been endeavouring there from time to time to improve them; and they have long recognized that in order that the author of any dramatic composition, whether musical or otherwise, may be protected in the ownership of his own work, it is necessary to prescribe criminal penalties for any theft thereof. I have not been able to find anything in this legislation that will afford similar protection to any man the product of whose brain may be ruthlessly stolen. It is not in any carping spirit but for the purpose of obtaining information which I should be glad to have that I am inquiring wherein the bill as now before us proposes to protect an author who may be ruthlessly pillaged and stolen from just as a man may have his bank account or anything else that belongs to him plundered by any unprincipled thief. I cannot see anything in the act with this object in view, and if my hon. friend will be good enough to point it out I shall be very grateful to him.

The Copyright Act as it now stands on the statute book provides in section 20 for civil remedies, that is to say, actions for damages, We have inserted in this bill a clause which we shall reach in a few moments in which, with respect to civil remedies, we have widely extended the recourse available to the author. I will discuss it when we reach the section. The present act also provides, in section 25, for summary remedies, with certain penalties of fine and
Copyright Act

imprisonment which may be imposed for infringement of copyright. This bill does not attempt to widen the scope of those penal clauses. Personally, I think that if we can provide adequate civil remedies it is not necessary that we should increase the penalties under the criminal law of Canada. If new penalties of fine and imprisonment are to be introduced, my own view is that they should be introduced as amendments to the criminal code. In any case, my hon. friend is correct to this extent, that we have imposed no new penalties in this bill. We have, however, preserved all the old penalties; they are there, untouched. And we have made civil remedies available to the author.

I did not intend to discuss this point just at the moment, but since the hon. gentleman has brought the question to the attention of the committee I may deal with it. I would much rather discuss it under clause 7, however.
Suppose we restrain our debate on the question until we reach that section.

I think that course would be wisest. I may say, however, that the law, as it stands at present in section 26 of the act, has proved absolutely worthless in the past as a remedy. And this bill, by clausa 7, does not make it any better-in fact, it is worse. I shall demonstrate that under clause 7.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-"-Copyright" further defined.

Section 3 of the bill incorporates two new sections into the Copyright Act in order that our act may conform, first, in clause (e), with article 14 of the convention which will be found on -page 12. Then clause (f) introduces an amendment in order to conform with article 11 bis of the convention. Article 11 bis reads:
(1) Authors of literary and artistic works shall enjoy the exclusive right of authorizing the communication of their works to the public by radio communication.
That is a new clause in the Rome convention which did not appear in the Beme convention, and in order that the clause may be enforced we have introduced in clause 3 a new clause (f) which reads:
In ease of any literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, to communicate such work by radio communication.
Section 3, in other words, is intended to bring our Copyright Act into conformity with

the Rome convention which it is proposed that Canada shall ratify.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-Cases -of joint ownership.

Section 4 is amended by the words underlined in the bill in order that our Copyright Act should conform to article 7 bis of the Rome -convention. The Berne convention provided that copyright should subsist during the lifetime of an author and in the case of joint authors, during the lifetime of the author who died first. This change will enact that a copyright shall subsist for fifty years from the date of the death of the joint author who dies last.

Section agreed to.
On section 5-Author's right to restrain acts prejudicial to his honour or reputation.

This section is introduced so that our statutory enactment known as the Copyright Act shall hereafter conform to article 6 Ibis of the Rome convention. Article 6 bis of the -convention reads:
Independently of the author's copyright, and even after transfer of the said copyright, the author shall have the right to claim authorship of the work, as well as the right to object to any distortion, mutilation or other modification of the said work which would be prejudicial to his honour or reputation.
That clause was introduced into -the convention of Rome to provide that, although an author had assigned -his entire right to a copyright, nevertheless he, being the author, has a moral right to safeguard his reputation against any distortion, mutilati-on or other modification of the said work. The convention uses the words "as well as the right to object," and we have incorporated the same provision into this bill with the insertion of the words "to restrain." The words "to object" would have no legal significance in the procedure of our courts and therefore the words "to restrain" are introduced into the bill in order to enable an author who has parted with his entire right to -a copyright to -proceed in our courts by means of injunction to restrain any such distortion, mutilation or other modification.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out that this is one of the important sections of the new bill. It recognizes the moral right of the author, and is one of the most important decisions arrived at in the convention at Rome. Perhaps I may be pardoned if I remind the -committee that at last session the government tried to deal with this very -matter by means of Bill

Copyright Act
No. 37, which acknowledged the moral right oif the author in such a way as has been pointed out by my hon. friend. Subsection 2 of article 6 bis of the convention reads as follows:
The determination of the conditions under which these rights shall be exercised is reserved for the national legislation of the countries of the union. The means of redress for safeguarding these rights shall be regulated by the legislation of the country where protection is claimed.
Bill No. 37, introduced last year, went farther than the present bill. It mentioned a fine not to exceed fifty dollars and costs and made provision for the redress mentioned in the convention. However, if the committee has followed me, it will have found out that while the convention is very precise in its declaration of principle, it leaves to the legislatures of the different countries the task of determining the means of redress and the penal provisions which must be attached to a copyright bill, as it is here. The Secretary of State will bear me out when I say that no effort has been made in the present bill to change the penal conditions of the Copyright Act. I share the views of the hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell) and my confrere from Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) that the act would probably bear a certain degree of amendment in that connection. It must be acknowledged that no effort is being made to touch upon these points, and perhaps these matters will be touched upon when we are discussing other clauses of the bill. It would be an appropriate task for a future session to deal with the penal conditions of the Copyright Act. However, as I said in my preliminary remarks on section 1, this bill is a step in the right direction. I know that no act is perfect, and. I am supporting this bill with the reservation of future discussion. I congratulate the Secretary of State upon having included clause 5 as I think the acknowledgment of the moral right of the author is well worth while. It is possible that hon. gentlemen on both sides of the house will be raising this penalty question, but perhaps they should be patient in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, as has
been so ably said, clause 5 of the bill is one of its most important features. However, I cannot let the occasion pass without stating how, when and where that important feature of the Rome revision came about. In 1925 a select committee of this house was appointed to investigate the Copyright Act. As a result of its deliberations, the committee brought forward a recommendation that the right of the author should be rec-22110-153
ognized in the way in which it is now defined, namely, as a "moral right". In 1926, a very able and esteemed member of this house, Mr. Ladner, introduced Bill No. 3, and for the first time in any legislature of the world the moral right of the author was recognized. That bill did not go through. In Mr. Ladner's bill, the moral right was defined as "the author's personal privilege of enjoying the prestige or influence which he may derive or which would accrue to him from his work notwithstanding any assignment of his .property rights". There is not a vast difference between that definition and the definition which was accepted in Rome; but the seed was not sown in vain; and I want to say on the floor of this house that it is to Canada's credit that this moral right has been introduced into a measure of international legislation. Because of that I feel very keenly on this matter. If the Rome convention has seen fit in its wisdom to embody that in its revision and then to make a special declaration to that effect, I say that it is highly incumbent upon Canada after having suggested the creation of this right, to see that it be properly protected. I am not prepared to admit, and I shall not admit, that there is in the present bill, or in any sections of the law as it stands to-day, anything that can be made applicable as a means of redress or safeguard in so far as moral right is concerned. Moral right is a new creation, and just as when we create statutory penal crimes we always by proper legislation, enacted at the same time, create the . adequate remedy, we should do so in this case. The convention has seen fit to prescribe it, and, wisely so, has left it to the respective contracting countries to devise the means to safeguard it. But the convention did not simply recognize the principle; it went further than that. I read subsection 2 of article 6 bis of the convention:
The determination of the conditions under which these rights shall be exercised is reserved for the national legislation of the countries of the union. The means of redress for safeguarding these rights shall be regulated by the legislation of the country where protection is claimed.
I repeat:
The means of redress for safeguarding these rights shall be safeguarded-
And permeating through nearly every article of the convention, as I shall show later on, there are imperative directions upon the contracting nations to enact such means of redress as will safeguard the rights of an author not only in his own country but also in other countries which are members of the union. For these reasons I cannot accept this section as it .'stands.

I think every true student of copyright in the first instance would frown upon such provisions as are contemplated in this section, and in that respect I desire to state my position very clearly. I believe personally that copyright is an absolute right, and that it is not for the statute but for the composer himself or the owner of the copyright to decide what use shall be made of his own music without his permission. That to my mind is the true principle of copyright. It is not for the state to decide that a church, a college or a fair shall be allowed to use music without cost or without acknowledgment of the copyright. It is for the owner of the copyright himself, or for the author to decide that. With reference to the new proposed subsection 3, under the law as it exists at present any plaintiff who comes into court and says that he is the author is presumed to be the author without proof. That presumption has not been changed. Paragraph (a) of subsection 3 says:
The work shall, unless the contrary is proved, he presumed to be a work in which copyright subsists.
Paragraph (b) says:
The author of the work shall, unless the contrary is proved, be presumed to be the owner of the copyright.
A new provision is inserted with respect to that presumption. If the copyright is registered and assignments of the copyright have been registered under the act, the succeeding presumptions are annulled if contrary to the registration which exists. It is simply to make that clear that lines fourteen, fifteen and sixteen on page 3 have been inserted. With regard to the new subsection 4, under the law as it exists to-day in the United Kingdom and under the law as it exists in Canada, the author or owner of a copyright must elect as to whether he will sue for damages or whether he will sue for participation in the profits made by the infringer of the copyright. One action excludes the other entirely. Actions are brought for damages, and no damage can be proven. Then an entirely new action has to be brought, within the term within which an action may be brought, for participation in the profits which may have been made by the infringer. The matter was discussed in the United States. The new copyright bill of the United States congress, which passed the House of Representatives, and passed its two readings in the senate but was lost because of a filibuster which prevented its third reading before the recent adjournment of congress, contained this section which was demanded iby the authors of the United States, namely, that in the same suit the author or owner cou'ld sue not only for damages but for participation in the profits made
by the infringer. It applies largely to broadcasting rights by radio. It is sometimes difficult for the author or owner to prove any substantial damages. This section provides that he may sue for damages and also for participation in profits, and that in addition to the. damages proved, the court may award him such share of the profits as the court may deem equitable. It goes further in favour of the author, and provides with regard to proving profits that all he is compelled to prove is the amount of revenue derived by the inifringer, and every element of cost which enters into the consideration of the question of profits must be proved by 'the infringer himself. This was inserted in the United States bill at the request of the authors of that country, and was finally approved by the senate unanimously without division. In view of the fact that in England and in this country the same difficulty arises, we deemed it advisable to give by this section to the author or owner the right to take conjoint action in respect of the two remedies which under our present system are mutually exclusive.

In Canada we have a Copyright Act. That act is derived from the British act, and pretty nearly everything in the way of remedy and means of redress to safeguard the author has been for some reason or other left out. The result is that the author has been pruned of almost all rights and means of redress and safeguards which to-day are provided for in the British act. Why should we have a sort of hybrid act, which is neither one nor the other? Between the two the author finds his defeat. In England to-day, there are a number of statutes that are operative in the British act, and which were scrupulously cut out of the Canadian law.
