On section 10-Performing rights.

I dislike very much to take up the time of the house, but as this section of the bill will be subject to discussion, I wish to -explain my position with regard to it. There is in this country a company known as the Performing Right Society of Canada. It was that company which brought to the attention

Copyright Act

of the government of the United Kingdom, the old section 40 of the Copyright Act as it exists at present. That section imposed upon any assignee of a grant or licence of performing rights the duty of producing at the Copyright office the original assignment and a duplicate of that assignment for registration. There must be duplicate copies of the assignment and unless the assignment was registered, no recovery could be made in respect of infringements of the act. It was found that duplicate copies were not in existence for many of those assignments which had been made during the past fifty years. In many cases the assignors had long since died and it was represented to the government of the United Kingdom 'by the Performing Right Society of England that it was unjust and unfair to exclude these assignments from registration owing to the impossibility of producing duplicate assignments from an assignor who had long since died. Secondly, in every case in which that company brought suit in respect of an infringement of a copyright they were compelled to show that the assignment of that copyright had been registered. They represented that they owned performing rights in 3,000,000. works; that the copyright office imposed a fee of one dollar in respect of each assignment, and that therefore the registration of their 3,000,000 works necessitated payment to the Copyright office of the sum of $3,000,000 for registration. It was in that connection that the communication came to the late government signed by Lord Lovat on behalf of the dominions' office in London. We have met that. It is no longer necessary that assignments should be made in duplicate; it is no longer necessary that assignments should be registered at all as a condition precedent to a recovery of damages for an infringement of copyright, or for the recovery of fees or royalties for performing rights. We have now by these sections which have passed, if they receive the final approval of parliament, wiped out all those objections. But this condition exists in Canada to-day: The Performing Right Society have hitherto been compelled to restrict their recovery of royalties, fees or charges for performing rights, to the few works which they have been able to register; but the Performing Right Society of England, which was the subject of investigation in that country in 1930, has procured the incorporation of a company in Canada known as the Performing Right Society of Canada Limited, with its head

office in Toronto. This company has procured from the English company an assignment of all its performing rights. It has procured from a similar association in France an assignment of all its performing rights; the same from Italy, the same from Germany, and more recently, from the United States it has procured an assignment of practically all performing rights in that country. The result is to-day that the Performing Right Society of Canada Limited controls the performance in 'Canada of the musical works of some 30.000 authors and musical works to the number of 3,000,000. It is admitted in their own testimony before the committee they control performing rights in. from 90 to 95 per cent of all modern music in the world. This Performing Right Society which has acquired this monopoly, I might say a super-monopoly, because each author has a monopoly in respect of his own works, has obtained vested rights in and control of about 95 per cent of all modern music, and instead of exacting fees and royalties as in times past for the performance of one musical work or a dozen musical works, it is now proposed to the users of music in Canada that they shall obtain from it a licence authorizing the performance of the whole 3,000,000 works, so that as at present, according to its present tariffs, which have been placed before the committee, if a band in a country community centre desires to perform band music, it must acquire from this company the right to perform the three million works which this society controls. If a broadcasting company, such as we find in Toronto or Montreal, desires to broadcast certain music as a part of the entertainment which it gives by radio, it is compelled to come to this company and pay whatever fee or royalty they demand, not for the performance of the 150 works which the broadcasting company may desire to perform, but for the performance of the whole three miilion works, or any of them or all of them which this society controls. Objection has been made to that. Very serious objection has been made by the broadcasting companies in this country, which I need not name, by the Canadian National Railways, which does a certain amount of broadcasting, by the Canadian Pacific Railway, which also broadcasts, and also by newspaper companies, which broadcast programs in various parts of this country. They have protested against that. Every hotel in this country which for the

Copyright Act
amusement and entertainment of its guests during the dinner hour performs music on the piano or by violin or by an orchestra is compelled to take monthly licences from the Performing Right Society of Canada for the performance of that music, and not for the performance simply of the 100 or 150 pieces which they may desire to perform during the week or month, but for the performance of the three million pieces which this company controls. Nearly every hotel proprietor in this country has protested against that condition of affairs. Exactly the same protests have come from civic bands, military and militia bands, and bands in certain civic communities throughout this country. If we amend this section 40 so that registration and the payment of fees under the act is no longer necessary, we no longer compel them to register their assignments, or the grants under which they obtained these rights; we no longer compel them to pay the fee of one dollar with respect to each registration, which will amount to $3,000,000. We give them all of that. But we wish to know the names of the pieces which this society controls. We say to them that it is in the interests of the music-users of this country that they should file in some public office in this country a list of the works which they control so that they are no longer in. a position to impose upon the people of this country the idea that they control everything. We say to them: File a list of the music works which you do control, so that those desiring to perform music may deal with other owners with respect to the works which they control. That they have so far refused to do.
Secondly, we say this; You do not represent the authors within the meaning and intent of the Berne convention or of the Rome convention. Those authors were granted certain rights with respect to their individual works. They were given the right of assignment of the copyright in those works. But an entirely new condition has arisen, where one society may control three million works, 95 per cent of the modern music of the world, and if that society is left unregulated and uncontrolled it is in the position of a combine or monopoly which in its own discretion may impose any royalties, any charges, any fees, whioh it may deem expedient, upon the music users of this country.
As to the method of control, we propose this provision:
Each association, society or company which carries on in Canada the business of acquiring copyrights of dramatico-musical or musical 22110-134i
works or of performing rights therein, and which deals with or in the issue or grant of licences for the performances in Canada of dramatico-musical or musical works in which copyright subsists, shall, from time to time, file with the minister at the copyright office:-
(a)	Lists of all dramatico-musical and musical works, in respect of which such association, society or company claims authority to issue or grant performing licences or to collect fees, charges or royalties for in resneet of the performance of such works in Canada; and
(b)	Statements of all fees, charges or royalties which such society, association or company proposes from time to time or at any time to collect in compensation for the issue or grant of licences for or in respect of the performance of such works in Canada.
That imposes upon them the duty of filing a list of their works, without charge, so that the public may be informed of what they control; and secondly, of filing a list of the fees, charges or royalties which they demand from the users of these musical works. Then comes the provision:
2. Whenever in the opinion of the minister, after an investigation and report by a commissioner appointed under the Inquiries Act, any such society, association, or company which exercises in Canada a substantial control of the performing rights in dramatico-musical or musical works in which copyright subsists, unduly withholds the issue or grant of licences for or in respect of the performance of such works in Canada, or proposes to collect excessive fees, charges or royalties in compensation for the issue or grant of such licences, or otherwise conducts its operations in Canada in a manner -which is deemed detrimental to the interests of the public-
Then, upon an inquiry and report showing that in either one. of these three ways the company is acting in a manner detrimental to the public interest, a revision may be made of the fees, charges and royalties which it imposes. Public sentiment in this country requires that. In my personal opinion that clause is within and consistent with the terms of the Berne convention and of the Rome convention because, while this country of Canada may adhere to such a convention for the protection of authors' rights, it certainly reserves its own inherent right to deal with a monopoly within this country which controls 95 per cent of a product, and which is free without such regulation to exact any such fees, royalties or other charges as it may in its discretion impose. This imposes no penalties upon such company. It simply says to them: There are certain limits within which you may impose fees, charges and royalties, but if you proceed in such a manner as is deemed subversive of the public interest, an inquiry may be held
